root_motivation: A team running several agents (visions/mcphost-killer-apps.md, component 5) has no place those agents can all write to and search short of standing up a database or a vector store and wiring auth for each agent: agents repeat work and contradict each other, and mcphost's group primitive (host.group.*, gating shared tools, src/sharing.rs) has no example beyond sharing a single http-kind wrapper (examples/share-a-tool). This PRD ships one owner-tenant memory table plus two shared python tools (remember/recall) as an llms.txt recipe, a three-tenant proof, and a synthorg task -- with zero mcphost code changes: the recipe composes host.table.*/host.tool_share/host.group.* exactly as they already exist.
user_persona: Four (PRD User stories): (1) the owner's agent creates the memory table, publishes and shares remember/recall, and adds two teammates; (2) a teammate's agent remembers something and a different teammate's recall returns it with the first teammate's id as writer; (3) the owner removes one member and that member's recall fails with a permission error while the other's keeps working; (4) Joe's synthetic panel measures time to the first cross-agent recall.

acceptance_criteria.description: Given llms.txt, When the section is read, Then it lists the table, two tools, group creation, two shares, and the add call, under 70 lines.

Given three fresh tenants set up per the section, When tenant B calls remember, Then the row exists in the owner's memory table with writer = B's tenant id (the documented who fallback, stated in examples/team-memory/proof.sh's own WRITER= output line).
Given B's row, When tenant C calls recall "deploy", Then the row is returned newest first with B as writer.
Given the owner removes C from the group, When C calls recall, Then a permission error is returned and B's recall still succeeds.
Given recall with limit 500, When called, Then at most 50 rows are returned.
Given the proof runs against https://mcphost.dev/mcp, When it finishes, Then AC2-5 hold and wall time is printed. (Live)

scope: www/llms.txt: new '## Give your agents one memory' section (53 lines) between the 'Share a tool, not a key: public variant' subsection and '## Limits and pricing' -- host.table.create(memory), two host.tool_publish calls (remember/recall, kind python), host.group.create, two host.tool_share calls, host.group.add, and a closing paragraph naming what `writer` holds and the `who` fallback.

examples/team-memory/proof.sh (new): three fresh tenants tagged x-mcphost-synthetic: recipe:team-memory (requirement 4); owner creates the table, publishes and shares remember/recall, adds B and C; B remembers; C recalls and sees B as writer; owner removes C; C's next recall errors while B's still succeeds; wall time printed. Mirrors examples/share-a-tool/proof.sh's helper shape (mcp_call/structured_of/json_str/has_error), plus a new mcp_call_ready retry wrapper for the python-kind tool_building cold-start window.

examples/team-memory/tools/remember.py, recall.py (new): the two shared python tools proof.sh publishes verbatim from these files. remember requires a caller-supplied `who` (mcphost does not expose the calling tenant's own id to a shared python tool -- CallCtx.tenant_id/namespace in src/kinds/mod.rs and every dispatch site in src/handler.rs carry only the OWNING tenant) and appends {key,text,tags,writer,at} via mcphost.table.append. recall builds a parameter-free SELECT (mcphost.table.query has no bind-param API -- src/kinds/python.rs's _table_query(sql) takes raw SQL text only), escaping the caller's query for SQL single-quotes and double-quoting the `key`/`text` column names, LIKE-matching key/text/tags, ORDER BY at DESC, rowid DESC, LIMIT clamped to 50 server-side regardless of the caller's requested limit (AC5); returns {rows, found} (`found` feeds the synthorg task's gold.call_check).

examples/team-memory/tools/forget.py (new, P2 requirement 7 / AC9 only -- not part of the P0 recipe in llms.txt or proof.sh): bakes the owner's own namespace in as OWNER_NAMESPACE at publish time (a shared tool has no other way to learn its own owner's identity from inside the sandbox), refuses (raises PermissionError, surfacing as tool_exception) unless the caller-supplied `who` matches the row's writer or OWNER_NAMESPACE. mcphost.table has no row-level delete/update (create/append/query/list/drop/schema only -- src/tables.rs's six pub async fns), so an authorized forget records a tombstone in a companion memory_forgotten table rather than deleting.

examples/team-memory/synthorg-task.yaml (new): one task, segment ops_coordinator, gold.tool_name=recall / gold.kind=python / gold.call_check="result.found == true" -- proposed addition for RedBaron's corpus (not merged into it, same cross-repo-scope note as share-a-tool's own synthorg-task.yaml).

additional.zero_mcphost_code_changes: Engineering target states this explicitly: no src/**/*.rs edit is part of this PRD's scope. Every requirement is met by composing host.table.*/host.tool_share/host.group.* exactly as they exist today, from python tool source and shell/docs/tests.
additional.writer_is_self_reported: The PRD's own load-bearing open question -- confirmed by reading src/kinds/mod.rs's CallCtx struct and every TenantTableBridge/TenantStateBridge construction site in src/handler.rs: CallCtx.tenant_id/namespace always carry the OWNING tenant, never the cross-tenant caller's, for a shared tool dispatched through call_cross_tenant_tool. remember/forget therefore take a caller-supplied `who` and trust it; www/llms.txt's own section states this plainly, and the fallback is not a security boundary -- group membership (checked at call time, src/sharing.rs) is what actually gates who can call the tool at all.
additional.no_row_level_delete: mcphost.table's pseudo-module (src/kinds/python.rs) and its host-side TableBackend (src/tables.rs) expose exactly six ops -- create/append/query/list/drop/schema -- with no delete-row or update-row op. forget.py therefore tombstones into a companion memory_forgotten table instead of deleting; adding a real delete op would violate zero_mcphost_code_changes above.

five_whys_trace.q: Why do a team's agents repeat work and contradict each other today?
five_whys_trace.a: They have no place they can all write to and search short of standing up a database or vector store and wiring auth for each agent -- too much for what's often a handful of short notes.

five_whys_trace.q: Why can't mcphost's existing group-sharing primitive (host.group.*, src/sharing.rs) already serve this?
five_whys_trace.a: It has no example beyond examples/share-a-tool -- a single http-kind wrapper around one owner's paid API key. Nothing demonstrates sharing a *stateful*, multi-writer python tool, or what a shared tool sees of who is calling it.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does a shared, multi-writer tool need anything beyond host.tool_share + host.table.*, both of which already exist?
five_whys_trace.a: Because every row needs to record who wrote it (Goal 2), and a shared tool executes in the OWNER's tenant context (src/sharing.rs, CallCtx.tenant_id) -- the open question was whether that context also carries the CALLER's identity.

five_whys_trace.q: Why does that open question matter enough to gate the design?
five_whys_trace.a: If the host exposed the real caller id, `writer` could be trustworthy by construction; since it does not (confirmed against src/kinds/mod.rs and src/handler.rs at build time), `writer` is only as trustworthy as the calling agent's own honesty about a caller-supplied `who` -- a real, stated limitation, not a bug, and the PRD's own technical considerations anticipated exactly this branch ("falls back to a caller-supplied who").

five_whys_trace.q: Why is a synthorg task and a wall-time-printing proof.sh part of this PRD rather than left to a follow-on?
five_whys_trace.a: Goal 1 promises "three tenants share one memory within 3 minutes on the free plan" and User story 4 asks Joe's synthetic panel to measure time to first cross-agent recall -- neither claim is real until something actually times it, the same reasoning examples/share-a-tool/proof.sh's WALL_TIME_MS line and its own synthorg-task.yaml already established as this repo's convention for a landed recipe.

ambiguities_resolved.resolution: Fixed in place, same 'amend the paper trail without reopening the contract' pattern used for every prior recurrence: no reviewer block yet, but the same staleness would recur if left byte-for-byte. root_motivation/scope/non_goals/user_persona/five_whys_trace/hard_constraints.additional were rewritten from this PRD's own Problem statement, Goals, Non-goals, User stories, and Technical considerations sections; acceptance_criteria's ten entries (this PRD numbers AC1-10, one more than the previous card) point at the real tests/wasmkind_ac0[1-9]_*.rs / tests/wasmkind_ac10_*.rs files, all of which exist, compile, and pass, with levels taken verbatim from the PRD's own Acceptance criteria list (AC1-7 and AC10 are P0/MUST, AC8-9 are P1/SHOULD); agent/test-map.json's ac_test_map was repointed to a new `wasmkind` prefix and the prior `sharetool` mapping preserved under ac_test_map_by_prefix (already present) rather than deleted. On the size-cap open question: this slice ships one global component-size cap (47 KiB / 48128 bytes) rather than a per-plan one -- sized empirically so the largest real fixture (the oom guest, which unavoidably links the full wasi:cli world via the Rust std allocator's abort path even though the guest code itself never touches sockets/filesystem) clears it with margin, while a spec at just over the bound still stays under the pre-existing global 64 KiB spec-storage cap once base64-encoded, so AC2's 'refused with a structured error naming the bound' proof doesn't collide with a second, unrelated cap. No other kind in this codebase varies its own size/resource limits per plan today, so introducing that axis only for wasm was judged out of scope for this slice and left to a follow-on PRD (recorded in non_goals) rather than guessed at without a plans.toml precedent to follow. Requirement 9 (P2, a corpus-task proposal) has no corresponding entry in the PRD's own ten-item Acceptance criteria list, so it was left out of this build's scope entirely rather than attempted without a proof to satisfy -- consistent with every other PRD-specific ambiguity resolution in this card's history choosing the PRD's own AC list as the actual contract, not the fuller Requirements table.

ambiguities_resolved.resolution: Fixed in place, same 'amend the paper trail without reopening the contract' pattern used for every prior recurrence: no reviewer block yet, but the same staleness would recur if left byte-for-byte. root_motivation/user_persona/scope/non_goals/hard_constraints.additional/five_whys_trace were rewritten from this PRD's own Problem statement, Requirements, Non-goals, and Technical considerations sections; acceptance_criteria's ten entries point at the real tests/mcphost_data_retention_ac0[1-9,10]_*.rs files (AC1-6 exist, compile, and pass; AC7 is 'deferred' with no test file, matching the PRD's own AC7 wording that its proof is a live trailer read, not a build-time test; AC8-10 exist, compile, and pass); agent/test-map.json's ac_test_map was repointed to a new `retention` prefix and the prior `wasmkind` mapping preserved under ac_test_map_by_prefix (already present) rather than deleted. On the two build-time decisions: (1) `calls_resource_usage` is tracked in `retention_policy` (its own env-configurable window, `MCPHOST_RETENTION_CALLS_RESOURCE_USAGE_DAYS`, listed in host.usage/admin.usage the same as every other table) but has no entry in `retention::EXECUTABLE_TABLES` -- pruning `calls` by the `calls` window already deletes those same rows' `cpu_ms`/`peak_rss_kb` columns, so there is nothing left to independently delete under a second name; this is recorded in `PolicyTable`'s own doc comment, not silently dropped. (2) AC7 is listed as MUST (matching the PRD's own P0 marking) but deferred with no test, consistent with how this card's history already treats a PRD's own explicitly-live AC (see the share-a-tool-not-a-key entry above for AC6's identical shape) -- the coder dispatch instructions' own acceptance list confirms this by asking only for it to be named under `deferred` with a one-line reason, not built a mock for.

ambiguities_resolved.question: This card is now regenerated for PRD-mcphost-tenant-data-export, an entirely different feature (a tenant data-export job) from PRD-mcphost-data-retention (per-table retention pruning) that previously occupied it -- root_motivation, acceptance_criteria, scope, non_goals, user_persona, five_whys_trace, and hard_constraints.additional all needed a full rewrite, the same staleness class caught by reviewer-agent at least ten times in this card's own history (see the entries above) if left byte-for-byte. This PRD also carries its own Open Questions table with one entry due 'at build', owner Joe: 'Archive size cap per plan (assumed: free 50 MB, pro 1 GB)'. Two further ambiguities needed a build-time decision with no PRD text to settle them directly: (1) the technical considerations name 'the tenant's scratch quota' and 'the existing session-key material' for the signed URL, but neither concept exists anywhere in this codebase (`tenant_state.rs` has only a KV byte quota, and there is no prior signed-URL/session-key secret at all); (2) `runs.rs`'s executor only ever dispatches a `queued` run through a tenant's published `Kind`, but an export has no `Kind` to dispatch through.
ambiguities_resolved.resolution: Fixed in place, same 'amend the paper trail without reopening the contract' pattern used for every prior recurrence: no reviewer block yet, but the same staleness would recur if left byte-for-byte. root_motivation/scope/non_goals/user_persona/five_whys_trace/hard_constraints.additional were rewritten from this PRD's own Problem statement, Goals, Non-goals, User stories, and Technical considerations sections; acceptance_criteria's seven entries point at the real tests/mcphost_tenant_data_export_ac0[1-3,5-7]_*.rs files (AC4 is Live, deferred, same convention as prior PRDs' own Live ACs -- see the share-a-tool-not-a-key entry above), with levels taken verbatim from the PRD's own P0/P1/P2 groupings (P0 -> MUST, P1/P2 -> SHOULD, no MUST-level regression risk since none of P1/P2 here guard an existing behavior). agent/test-map.json's ac_test_map was repointed to a new `tenantdataexport` prefix and the prior `retention` mapping preserved under ac_test_map_by_prefix (already present) rather than deleted. On the three build-time decisions: the size-cap open question shipped as `Plan.export_bytes_max` with exactly the PRD's own assumed numbers (free 50 MiB, pro 1 GiB), tolerant-defaulted for a `plans.toml` predating the key, same convention as every other per-plan quota in that file. 'The tenant's scratch quota' was realized as that same new plan-level byte cap (checked against the built archive) rather than inventing a new storage primitive, with the archive itself written under the host's existing data dir (`Db::data_dir()`) since no per-tenant scratch filesystem exists to reuse. 'The existing session-key material' was resolved as each tenant's own `key_hash` column -- already stored server-side, unique per tenant, unguessable (SHA-256 of a 32-byte random key) -- keying the same from-scratch `billing::hmac_sha256` this crate already has, so the URL's HMAC needs no new secret. The dispatch-through-a-Kind gap was resolved by never enqueuing an export as `queued` at all: `Db::start_export_run` inserts it straight into `running` (atomically checking for an already-running export first, for AC3), invisible to `runs::tick`'s leasing loop by construction, with `export::run_export_job` the only thing that ever finalizes it.

ambiguities_resolved.question: PRD Open question (Technical considerations / Open questions table, owner "Joe / builder at step 1"): does the host expose the caller's tenant id inside a shared python tool today? The PRD's own branch: if not, `writer` falls back to a caller-supplied `who` and "the vision's open question gets a rust-extend follow-on." Separately, two build-time gaps had no PRD text to settle them directly: (1) requirement 7 (P2) asks for a `forget {id}` restricted to writer or owner, but mcphost.table has no row-delete op and Non-Goals forbids any python-kind/sharing code change to add one; (2) this coding sandbox's own ssh bin-shim ("ssh is never a build agent's to call", WM_BUILD_AGENT=1) rejects every `wm-build runner sync`/`exec` invocation this PRD's own build instructions named as the only way to run cargo, so `cargo test`/`cargo clippy` could not be executed from this session despite ~10 minutes and 7+ attempts (journal.jsonl's shim-rejected entries confirm this is a deterministic policy rejection, not network flakiness -- an earlier, successful exec-1.log entry for this same run predates this coder session and was performed by a different, unsandboxed process).
ambiguities_resolved.resolution: (1) Confirmed by reading src/kinds/mod.rs's CallCtx struct (tenant_id/namespace fields, no caller field) and every TenantTableBridge/TenantStateBridge/CallCtx construction site in src/handler.rs (call_published_tool's owner-tenant dispatch, call_cross_tenant_tool's group-membership check followed by the same owner-tenant CallCtx): the host does NOT expose the caller's tenant id to a shared python tool. root_motivation/scope/hard_constraints.additional above take the PRD's own documented-fallback branch: remember/forget take a caller-supplied `who`, www/llms.txt's own section states plainly what `writer` holds and that the fallback is not a security boundary (group membership, checked at call time by src/sharing.rs, is). No rust-extend follow-on PRD was opened by this build (out of scope for a coder session; noted here for the next PRD queued against this vision's open question). (2) forget.py tombstones into a companion memory_forgotten table (mcphost.table.append) rather than deleting, keeping requirement 7/AC9's refusal check real while adding no mcphost code. (3) Every file this PRD adds was written and locally reasoned through as carefully as this session could manage without cargo: each python tool source parses under `python3 -c 'import ast; ast.parse(...)'`, recall.py's SQL-building logic was exercised against a hand-rolled mock of mcphost.table.query (confirming escaping and the 50-row clamp), and every host-side API call (mcphost.table.create/append/query argument names, TableBackend op dispatch, AppError::Structured code propagation for table_already_exists) was checked directly against src/tables.rs/src/kinds/python.rs/src/handler.rs rather than assumed. `cargo test`/`cargo clippy` remain unrun from this session; this card and the coder's own final report both say so plainly rather than fabricating a 'test result:' line, so the next session with working runner access (or an operator unblocking this sandbox's ssh shim) has a clean, honest starting point.
